title.en: The Old Bachelor and the Flying Song

region.en: Coast firth and the mountain peak

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 52 'The Old Bachelor', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A bachelor who hates singing hears a boat going up the firth unrowed against the wind, singing 'Let us be taken aloft!' — lifted through the air with it, he stays with the flying household, learns their magic lay, and flies home with a victual-laden kayak. Pausing on a steep peak, he finds the song gone from his memory and tumbles down the precipice catching at words — 'immaketja! no... kinajaja! no, that's not it neither' — until the true verse returns an arm's length above the stone-heaps. He lands inside his own house, kayak-point crushing the wall, and that was his first and last journey through the air.
summary.zh: 討厭唱歌的老鰥夫聽見一艘逆風不用槳、憑歌上溯的船——『讓我們飛上天吧！』——他隨船凌空而去，寄住飛行人家、習得咒歌，載滿食物飛返家鄉。在陡峭山巔稍歇之際，歌詞忽然從記憶中消失；他一邊哭一邊抓住隻言片語往下滾落——直到離亂石堆一臂之遙才想起正句，凌空獲救。最後他駕艇直衝自家屋內，艇首撞上內牆——那是他第一次、也是最後一次的空中之旅。

sensitivity.note: Flying-boat song (kangatarsa) motif; documented as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: There was once a queer old bachelor who had a singular dislike to singing: whenever he heard people sing, he would take himself off immediately. One day, being out at his hunting-place off the coast, he heard people singing, and it proved to proceed from the crew of a boat which was going up the firth right against the wind, and without being rowed. This song pleased him; he went up to the boat, which he several times noticed to be lifted up into the air, soon to sink down again on the surface of the water, and constantly advancing, although the crew seemed resting on their oars all the while.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 52 'The Old Bachelor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He now asked leave to be one of the party; the steersman said he might follow them if he chose, but that he must keep close to them — they tied his kayak to the boat, and then continued singing, Kangatarsa, Kangatarsartigut! (let us be taken aloft!) imakaja, ah, ha, ha — they were instantly lifted up and taken away across the country. Being now on the top of a very high mountain they took a little rest, but soon after travelled on through the air until they alighted close beside a house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 52 'The Old Bachelor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He discharged the boat and got out of his kayak on land, entered a house to pay them a visit, came to like them, remained with them, and learned their magic song. But at length he bethought himself of his relatives, who were sure to be missing him and concerned about his fate, and resolved to return; his hosts proceeded to fill his kayak with victuals, after which he got in, and singing the magic lay, flew away in the same direction he had formerly come from — but when he reached the high mountain, he got a strong fancy to repose for a while on the summit of it, which happened to be a very steep peak. After a while he wanted to be off again, but found that he had suddenly forgotten the lay, and then he sat down all at a loss on the steep mountain-side; at last he lost his balance, and was about to fall down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 52 'The Old Bachelor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He tried to catch hold of the proper words, and sang, 'Immaketja!' — no; not quite that; 'Kinajaja!' — no, that's not it neither — and now he began crying and tumbling down the precipice. When he was quite close to the stone-heaps at the foot of the mountain he remembered the song, and was again carried through the air, and thus saved from destruction. At last he saw his dwelling-place, where his house-fellows had quite given him up for lost; they were just assembled outside when all at once they heard a song from above, and looking upwards perceived a kayaker overhead rushing through the air, and before long recognised their own old bachelor. He directed his course straight towards the entrance, never stopping until he sat right down on the ledge, his kayak's point crushing against the wall of the room — and this was his first and last journey through the air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 52 'The Old Bachelor'; not verbatim.

title.en: Salik the Kivigtok and His Namesake
title.zh: 奇維托克薩利克與同名者

region.en: Northern solitude and the great glacier

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 53 'Salik the Kivigtok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Ice-bound north, Salik returns for a forgotten axe and is surprised in the dark house by his own namesake — a clairvoyant scrap-gatherer who heard everything but his steps. The visitor tells his life: ten children fed plate after plate, a mother's words about a mother's-brother who fled mankind for his wife's scolding — words he could not swallow, so he ran into the interior, killed a buck in a snowstorm with a finger-length knife, matched his speed with any animal, hunted an amarok across the glacier clefts, and was entertained by little hare-women mocking the 'wicked little foxes' and the hare that sits down at the word itek. Paid with a knife from the boot, he ran off as swiftly as a flying raven.
summary.zh: 北地冰封，薩利克回頭取遺落的斧頭，卻在黑屋中被同名者撞見——一位先知的拾荒客，萬物之聲皆入其耳，唯獨聽不見腳步。客人自述一生：十個孩子一盤接一盤地吃；母親一句『我舅父就是被妻子罵了才遁世』的話哽在喉頭，使他奔入內陸；雪暴中以一指長的刀刃獵殺公鹿；練就與百獸賽跑的腳力；冰川裂隙間追逐狼靈阿馬洛克；又得兔化少女相伴，笑談『狡猾的小狐狸』與一聲『itek』便坐地不動的野兔。臨別，他自靴筒抽出一把小刀相贈，隨即如飛掠的渡鴉般疾奔而去。

sensitivity.note: Kivigtok clairvoyance and hare-women (transformation) motifs. Domestic quarrel origin of the flight recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Salik went off to the north; and during his journey the frost set in, and cut off his passage home, and he established himself for the winter at a very solitary place. The following spring he drew still farther north; after some hours' travelling he remembered that they had left their axe fixed in one of the cross-beams of their deserted house. He at once returned and entered the dark house through the open window; just as he was going to take hold of the axe he heard something moving about beside the ledge, down on the floor, and on looking more closely caught sight of a man. The stranger began to whistle aloud, but soon after spoke thus: 'Though I am always aware of what is going to happen, thou hast for once chanced to take me by surprise. This is the way in which I manage: being very quick, it is my wont to go about from one place to another, picking up odd scraps and leavings after people move away to other parts... I think it is the custom when meeting a man for the first time to ask him his name.' 'My name is Salik' — 'Why, so is mine; and since thou hast, to a certain degree, outdone me, who have never before been taken aback, I shall relate the history of my life to thee.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 53 'Salik the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: His history: ten children leaving the house every morning with their father, spending the day practising bow-shooting and flinging stones, fed plate after plate on their return — 'But we were ten children, and therefore the plate had to be filled thrice before we were quite satisfied.' One evening they found the lamps tumbled bottom-up, the parents' manners altered; the father said, 'These will probably be hungry: I am not going to do like my mother's brothers, who fled from mankind because he had been scolded by his wife' — and the mother replied, 'If he had any sense at all, he would not speak in that way.' The angmagsat-fishing, the dykes for the salmon, the lancing and drying — 'My brothers enjoyed that busy time; but I had not yet learned to forget those words of my mother's, and my spirits grew more and more depressed.' At the dam he turned to his youngest brother — 'I think I see a partridge yonder: pray take my lot of salmons along with thee while I pursue the bird' — and darting off, ran straight on for the interior, never stopping his flight till nightfall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 53 'Salik the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: All the summer he roamed about snaring partridges, and in the autumn built himself a house for the winter. One morning, in a terrible snow-fall, he saw a large male reindeer seeking food beneath the snow — dreadfully hungry, he could not suppress a loud cry on seeing it: 'The knife I have got here — showing a stump of a knife hardly a finger's-length — was then considerably longer: I took hold of it, and crept up to the animal very cautiously... rushing at it, thrusting my knife several times into its flanks, following up its bloody tracks until I got it killed' — a fat buck, providing him sufficiently for the winter. Next summer he travelled to a place abounding in those animals and became well skilled in hunting them, but constantly got very low-spirited, going in search of more daring excitement — he only happened to meet with some poor old kivigtut. He had got to be very nimble-footed, and could run a race with any animal that ever was.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 53 'Salik the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Once he ascended the highlands to the verge of the large glacier and climbed his way on to an ice-bound land; his boots poor and soaked, he took out the skin-stockings to dry — and surveying the immense plain, perceived a tiny black spot at some distance: a raven, then more like a fox, then the size of a reindeer, then like an amarok. Having all the time been in search of something appalling enough to rouse his dejected spirits, he resolved to front and attack the animal — on its approach, however, he found himself turning somewhat irresolute. The beast bent down, the ice flying about it on every side; it bounded right towards him, and he took to his heels trying to gain the ice where it was less smooth and slippery, thinking all his diversion would likely end in being devoured by a monster. He reached some large clefts in the ice — when obliged to leap, the monster merely took a long stride over — and looked out for a very wide crevice, thinking it would be quite as well to fall down the precipice as to be swallowed up by the beast. He barely managed to cross it; no sooner had he gained the other side than he heard a fearful yell, and turning round beheld the monster hanging perched on the edge of the icy rocks, unable to get up again. He sprang towards it, but before he had time to kill it, it was tumbling down the precipice — and thus he lost his prize. At the beginning of every winter he filled two storehouses with victuals, remembering the terrible want of the first winter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 53 'Salik the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One evening, seated at his work, he suddenly heard somebody passing through the entry, and two little women presently appeared before him, both light-haired with a cleft in their upper lips, each carrying a bag with berries — no room left in the little house when they sat down. He treated them civilly as his very first visitors; they poured out their berries and begged him to eat with them, and he brought in grease and meat, of which they would take nothing, being much amused at their lively talking all the evening through. 'When people don't keep an eye upon their stores, the wicked little foxes will come and carry them off; and then, when they happen to take them by surprise, they will run away, the tails turned right out' — laughing till out of breath; he joined their merry laughter and felt very happy indeed. At length they left him, taking their bags, and he now perceived for the first time that his guests had been hares disguised in the shape of women. Another evening two other little women entered — darker complexion, larger tufts of hair, still more amiable: 'These silly little hares, whenever they happen to meet folks, they sit down staring at them — they look so very funny with their cloven lips; and when they take to run, and people only say itek, they sit down on the spot.' 'Now I have got practised in running, and skip about from place to place whenever I know that people have newly left. Accordingly I came here. Thou alone hast taken me by surprise; otherwise I seem to hear everything. When the partridges sit down yonder behind the high mountain-ridges, I shall be sure to hear them as if they were quite close by: but thy steps I have not heard.' From the upper part of his boot the first Salik produced a knife and handed it to the narrator — 'I have got nothing else wherewith to pay thee back the pleasure thou hast given me.' 'I feel a little indisposed immediately after the meal, but just follow me with a look' — and off he ran, up the high sloping hill as swiftly as a flying raven that soars smoothly along, barely touching the earth, and thus quickly out of sight; Salik often repeated the interesting tale of his namesake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 53 'Salik the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.
